title: Growing Hypergraphs with Edge Copying

2-edge motifs in hypergraphs
Claim: What’s special about the structure of hypergraphs is that they have diverse, undirected, two-edge motifs: intersections.

title: Growing Hypergraphs with Edge Copying
text:
Intersections in Temporal Hypergraphs


Let \(r_k^{(t)}\) be the probability that two uniformly random hyperedges which arrive before time \(t\) have an intersection of size \(k\).
In empirical hypergraphs, \(r_k^{(t)}\) often decays at rates close to \(t^{-1}\) or \(t^{-2}\), regardless of \(k\).
Benson, Abebe, Schaub, and Kleinberg (2018). Simplicial closure and higher-order link prediction. PNAS  Chodrow (2020). Configuration models of random hypergraphs. JCN  Landry, Young, and Eikmeier (2023). The simpliciality of higher-order networks. EPJ Data Sci.







Dashed lines give slope of \(t^{-1}\) and \(t^{-2}\) decay.

title: Growing Hypergraphs with Edge Copying
text:
Hyperedge Copy Model


Formally
In each timestep \(t\):

Start with an empty edge \(f = \emptyset\).
Select an edge \(e \in H\).
Accept each node from \(e\) into \(f\) with probability \(\eta\) (condition on at least one).

Add \(X \sim \boldsymbol{\beta}\) novel nodes.
Add \(Y \sim \boldsymbol{\gamma}\) nodes from \(H \setminus e\).

title: Growing Hypergraphs with Edge Copying
text:
Scalable online learning via stochastic EM

 
Aim: given the sequence of edges \(\{e_t\}\), estimate:

\(\eta\), the edge retention rate.
\(\beta\), the distribution of the number of novel nodes added to each edge.
\(\gamma\), distribution of the number of pre-existing nodes added to each edge.


Sample \(e_t\) and form a belief about seed edge \(f\).
Update a vector of expected sufficient statistics \(\theta_t\) and current parameter estimates \(\bar{\eta}\), \(\bar{\beta}\), and \(\bar{\gamma}\).
Repeat until tired.

We computed AUC scores for a link prediction task in which our model learns parameters on 20% training data from three metabolic and organic reaction data sets with edges up to size 5. We compared these against previously-reported AUC scores on the same task for two dedicated neural network hypergraph link prediction algorithms.

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Our Data




 

Ben Brill, UCLA ’22
Total of 116,306 advisor-student pairs in the US since 1950, representing 21,781 distinct advisors.  We observe or estimate math subfields for 94% of these pairs (predictions based on thesis titles).  We estimate gender for 95% of PhD students and 97% of advisors.

text: Modeling Gendered PhD Production by an Advisor

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Men have estimated careers ~4 years longer (on average)


Attrition
Addressing disparities in career attrition for female faculty would help to close the gender gap.

Qualitative match to Barrett-Walker et al. (2023).

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Longer careers \(\times\) more students per year = more students per career


Hypothesis: greater student production per year by male advisors reflects unequal access to research resources; cf. Zhang et al. (2022)

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Logistic model for advisee gender
Estimate the odds that the next student produced by an advsior is female based on subfield, advisor gender, and representation of women in advisor group and subfield.
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \log (\text{odds F}) = & \beta_0 \;+ &\quad \beta_0 &= -2.14 \; (0.04)\\
                         & \rho \times (\text{advisor is F}) \;+ &\quad\rho &= \phantom{-}0.42 \;(0.02)\\
                         & \gamma \times (\text{proportion F advisees in group}) \;+ &\quad \gamma &= \phantom{-}1.16\; (0.06)\\
                         & \eta \times (\text{proportion F in subfield})  &\quad \eta &= \phantom{-}3.27 \; (0.12)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
We tried a lot of more complex models; this one had best validation AUC.




Mentorship
Female advisors are more effective in attracting or retaining female graduate students.




Belonging
Greater representation in the grad student community attracts women to programs and subfields.

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Homophily effects: advisor-student and student-student

  
Both the gender of a students’ specific advisor and the overall proportion of female advisors in the subfield’s population contribute to the likelihood that the student is female.

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Modeling Interventions on Medium Timescales: Hiring


Equal hiring rates
Suggested in most recent AMS survey data.


Male-biased hiring
Men 20% more likely than women to be hired as faculty.


Female-biased hiring
Women 20% more likely than men to be hired as faculty.

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
Intervening on Attrition + PhD Production


No intervention
Attrition + PhD production as estimated by model.


Faculty Intervention
Gender parity among current faculty on attrition and PhD production.


Student Intervention
Gender parity among future students on attrition and PhD production.


Faculty + Student Intervention
Both interventions combined.

title: PhD Mentorship and Gender Representation in Academic Mathematics
text:
What We’ve Learned




Mentorship: Female advisors are more effective in attracting or retaining female graduate students.






Belonging: Representation in the grad student community attracts women to programs and subfields.






Attrition: Addressing disparities in career attrition for female faculty would help to close the gender gap.

title: Learning Social Influencewith Unobserved Mechanisms
text:
Learning the model






Our stochastic model defines a likelihood function over observed opinion trajectories, given an observation of a fixed network of possible interactions.



We learn the kernel parameters by maximizing this likelihood via the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977).



We select between competing models (kernels, mechanisms, etc.) by evaluating their predictive likelihoods on held-out validation data.

Discrepancy

Kernel

\(\delta = k(d) + \text{noise}\)



Outcome


The target’s opinion moves by \(\delta\)



Slide h/t Will Thompson

The toy numbers below about the sigmoid gain describe the old curve; the outcome panel still uses that run (same mean move at d, so the jump is consistent). [WILL: one dyad, built up in six clicks. Start from the opinion line [0, 1]; (1) the target’s opinion x_t; (2) a source x_s at discrepancy d. (3) The kernel k(d) says how far the target moves at that discrepancy. (4) The update: delta = k(d) + noise, a move toward the source plus zero-mean noise. (5) Outcome: the target’s opinion moves by delta, one step in a trajectory. This is the paper’s hero, piece by piece; retention and selection get added to it later]

Facts, with sources:

Notation: this slide absorbs both lambda and d into k, so the slide’s k(d) is the paper’s lambda k(|d|) d, the expected move. d = x_s - x_t. Linear (DeGroot) is a straight line through the origin, k(d) = lambda d. If asked: “in the paper k is a gain, and we split it into a scale lambda and a shape”. Every later slide uses the same k(d): #explanations and the hero kernel panels (#model-attention, #model-hero) draw the move against the discrepancy, not the gain [scripts/talk/scenes/_hero.py kernel_panel].
Toy numbers: x_t = 0.40, x_s = 0.70, d = 0.30, paper gain k(|d|) = 0.92, lambda = 0.75, so k(d) = 0.21 is the mean move; sigma = 0.035. The paper gain here is a sigmoid with half-point 0.6 and steepness 0.12, wider than the hero’s World (0.35, 0.07), so d sits on the rising flank of k [scripts/talk/scenes/_scene.py, World; panels/model_kernel.py].
The density p(delta) is scaled so its centre sits level with k(d) on the kernel [panels/model_kernel.py, kernel()].
The paper writes the update as delta_e ~ q(. | mu, eta) with mu = lambda k(|d_e|) d_e [Overleaf sections/method_v2.tex:52]; “noise” on the slide is q.
The noise around the mean move is one of the paper’s noise families; the talk holds it fixed (Laplace in the paper’s selected models) [paper Methods].

SFI
Information environments help shape the beliefs of individuals and populations. The question of how they do this–how social influence operates–has been a long-running concern of social psychologists and, more recently, mathematical modelers. In both experiments and models, researchers often assume that individuals are always susceptible to influence from every potentially salient element of their information environment simultaneously. The implied narrative is one in which a user opens Twitter and is immediately influenced by the opinions of every user they follow. Of course, the user is actually exposed only to a subset of recent posts, and may not be susceptible to influence by all of them. We introduce a model of social influence which explicitly represents an agent’s selective attention to their environment as an unobserved mechanism which shapes dynamics. This turns out to be a very impactful choice: modeling selective attention can qualitatively alter the findings of statistical inference on both synthetic and real data. It also turns out to be a helpful choice: models with latent mechanisms consistently outperform standard methods for fitting social influence functions on a wide range of empirical data sets ranging from controlled psychological studies, congressional political alignments, Reddit arguments, and prediction markets. We hope that this work contributes to a reexamination of some common assumptions in mathematical models and to the development of new directions in quantitative research on social influence.

BiCo
Information environments help shape the beliefs of individuals and populations. The question of how they do this–how social influence operates–has been a long-running concern of social psychologists and, more recently, mathematical modelers. In both experiments and models, researchers often assume that individuals are always susceptible to influence from every potentially salient element of their information environment simultaneously. The implied narrative is one in which a user opens Twitter and is immediately influenced by the opinions of every user they follow. Of course, the user is actually exposed only to a subset of recent posts, and may not be susceptible to influence by all of them.
In this talk, I’ll briefly survey some standard mathematical models of social influence with an eye towards their underlying mechanical assumptions. I’ll then introduce a new model of social influence in which we explicitly represent an agent’s selective attention to their information environment. Since we don’t usually get to directly observe attention in most experiments and data sets, we model this as a latent mechanism and develop an expectation-maximization algorithm for statistical inference. The incorporation of selective attention turns out to be a very impactful choice: incorporating selective attention can qualitatively alter the outcome of model selection on both synthetic real data. It also turns out to be a helpful choice in the context of statistical prediction. Models with latent mechanisms consistently outperform standard methods for fitting social influence functions on a wide range of empirical data sets ranging from controlled psychological studies, congressional political alignments, Reddit arguments, and prediction markets.

Adams 2022, n = 3,760 updates







Standard: average over all neighbors

title: Learning Social Influencewith Unobserved Mechanisms
text:
Many Kernels, Many Mechanisms


Linear
Compromise –> consensus


convergence

Empirical justification


Vande Kerckhove et al. 2016
Takács et al. 2016
Clemm von Hohenberg et al. 2017
Friedkin & Bullo 2017
Friedkin et al. 2021





Repulsion
Compromise with similar opinions, repulsed by distant opinions


polarization



Mazen & Leventhal 1972
van Knippenberg et al. 1990
Krizan & Baron 2007
Liu & Srivastava 2015





Bounded confidence
Compromise with similar opinions, ignore distant opinions


clusters


Moussaïd et al. 2013






Or do it nonparametrically!









Rahimi + Recht (2007)



[WILL: the first models said influence is linear: DeGroot, a flat kernel, every update a fixed fraction of the gap. Run that and everyone meets. Our world does not look like that; it is dominated by dissensus and polarization. So what kernel makes this world? Each kernel shape is a hypothesis about why we disagree, and each has its backers. Walk the columns left to right: the shape, who reports it, and the world it makes. Linear pulls everyone together; repulsion pushes far opinions away and leaves two poles; bounded confidence stops listening past a radius and leaves clusters. Same kind of experiment, every possible answer. Last click: no one agrees on the shape]
Three clicks: repulsion column, bounded confidence column, then the punch line. (2026-10-11: order swapped from BC then repulsion.)
Facts, with sources:

One curve per column, drawn as influence k(d) (each column on its own y scale; bounded confidence peaks at 0.045, just inside its radius), from the paper’s gain functions: DeGroot k = 1, the diagonal; hard bounded confidence, radius 0.15 (full gain inside, zero beyond: Deffuant/Hegselmann-Krause); SAR with crossover 0.4 [presentations/ccs_2026/panels/explanations.py; kernel_inference/paper_figures/kernel_gains.py].
Bottom row is simulated, not data: 60 agents, each step every agent hears one agent drawn at random and moves 0.3 k(d), clipped to [0, 1], 80 steps, seed 1. Linear ends in consensus, bounded confidence in clusters, repulsion in two poles at the edges [same].
Citations are Kozitsin (2021) Table 1, “Studies testing influence assumptions against real data”, by its three columns: linear positive, moderated positive, positive + negative. All approved (+) except Krizan & Baron 2007, which rejected the positive + negative hypothesis. Kozitsin’s footnotes, dropped from the slide: Mazen & Leventhal 1972 ignores trends in opinion shifts; van Knippenberg et al. 1990 does not separate in-group and out-group influence; Liu & Srivastava 2015 is nonlinear, with an increasing rate [~/Zotero/storage/2Q4MVCCW, Table 1].
Column headings are ours: Kozitsin’s “moderated positive” is influence that fades with distance, which is the bounded confidence shape; “positive + negative” is assimilation near, repulsion far.

Literature (verified 2026-10-05 against the papers where reachable; otherwise the manuscript):

Takács, Flache & Mäs 2016, PLoS ONE 11(6):e0157948: “positive and rather linear” (Study 1, distance coefficient 0.34); “We did not find support for the negative influence hypothesis.” One manuscript sentence (background.tex:10) calls Takács bounded confidence; that contradicts the paper.
Vande Kerckhove et al. 2016, PLOS ONE 11(6):e0157685: constant influenceability alpha per player; bounded confidence only mentioned as an alternative.
Kozitsin 2021, J. Math. Sociol. 46(1): positive shifts “largely through a linear form or an inverted U-shaped form”, hence in two columns. Its negative shifts “may be partially explained … without referring to the notion of repulsive influence”.
Deffuant et al. 2000; Hegselmann & Krause 2002: step kernels, theory only. DeGroot 1974: constant gain, theory. Noise destroys BC clusters: Pineda, Toral & Hernández-García 2009 [not re-verified].
Moussaïd et al. 2013, PLOS ONE 8(11):e78433: “Social influence is negligible when opinions are initially too distant.” The far zone is fading influence, not repulsion.
Sherif, Taub & Hovland 1958: assimilation near the anchor, contrast far from it. Latitudes of acceptance are Sherif & Hovland 1961, not 1958.
Adams et al. 2022, PLOS ONE 17(10):e0275473: the manuscript (introduction.tex:4) says it observed repulsive dynamics, reported as an anomaly. The paper itself tests the Martins model. [WILL: check before saying this out loud]
If asked about backfire in the field: Bail et al. 2018 (PNAS); failures to find it: Wood & Porter 2019, Guess & Coppock 2020 [not re-verified]. Mäs & Flache 2013, PLoS ONE 8(11):e74516: “bi-polarization can be explained without negative influence”.
Becker et al. 2017 left off: no kernel-shape claim found.

Folded in from the dissensus slide (#why-dissensus, now in backup), which showed a DeGroot consensus run against a bounded-confidence dissensus run and a tangle of candidate kernels with a question mark:

Its trajectory panels are simulated, not data: 60 agents, each step every agent hears one agent drawn at random and moves 0.3 k(d), clipped to [0, 1], 80 steps, seed 1. DeGroot, k = 1, ends in consensus. Sigmoidal bounded confidence (sharpness 200, squared radius 0.05, so radius 0.22) ends in two groups near 0.31 and 0.79, away from the edges: dissensus without extremes [panels/why_dissensus.py]. The linear column’s dynamics panel on this slide is the same consensus run.
DeGroot in the paper’s notation: k(|d|) = 1, so the mean move is lambda d.
Its tangle of candidate kernels was illustrative: sigmoidal BC at four radii, SAR at four crossovers, an inverted U and a concave decline; not a list of fitted kernels [panels/why_dissensus.py, CANDIDATES].
Picture options if the slide gets real data later: Voteview’s party means over time, or a protest photo shot from a distance with no identifiable faces.

Towards Formalization: [What Kind of







]{.alert-1} {#model-kernel}


Modeling one-to-one influence with interaction kernels



Discrepancy






0 inches 10 inches Opinion x: how much has the dot moved?

\(x_t\): opinion of the target \(x_s\): opinion of a source at discrepancy \(d\)



Kernel





The kernel \(k(d)\) sets how far the target moves
\(\delta = k(d) + \text{noise}\)



Outcome


The target’s opinion moves by \(\delta\)



Slide h/t Will Thompson


2026-10-11: kernel panel is now a mostly attractive kernel with a shallow repulsive dip (x(0.45-x), damped past the zero crossing at d = 0.45, dip about a quarter of the peak; x axis “similar” to “different”) with the #bipolarization shading: top half “I move toward you”, bottom half “I move away from you”. Scaled so k(d) at d = 0.3 equals the World’s mean move (0.21), so p(delta) shares the kernel’s y axis. The toy numbers below about the sigmoid gain describe the old curve; the outcome panel still uses that run (same mean move at d, so the jump is consistent). [WILL: one dyad, built up in six clicks. Start from the opinion line [0, 1]; (1) the target’s opinion x_t; (2) a source x_s at discrepancy d. (3) The kernel k(d) says how far the target moves at that discrepancy. (4) The update: delta = k(d) + noise, a move toward the source plus zero-mean noise. (5) Outcome: the target’s opinion moves by delta, one step in a trajectory. This is the paper’s hero, piece by piece; retention and selection get added to it later]

Facts, with sources:

Notation: this slide absorbs both lambda and d into k, so the slide’s k(d) is the paper’s lambda k(|d|) d, the expected move. d = x_s - x_t. Linear (DeGroot) is a straight line through the origin, k(d) = lambda d. If asked: “in the paper k is a gain, and we split it into a scale lambda and a shape”. Every later slide uses the same k(d): #explanations and the hero kernel panels (#model-attention, #model-hero) draw the move against the discrepancy, not the gain [scripts/talk/scenes/_hero.py kernel_panel].
Toy numbers: x_t = 0.40, x_s = 0.70, d = 0.30, paper gain k(|d|) = 0.92, lambda = 0.75, so k(d) = 0.21 is the mean move; sigma = 0.035. The paper gain here is a sigmoid with half-point 0.6 and steepness 0.12, wider than the hero’s World (0.35, 0.07), so d sits on the rising flank of k [scripts/talk/scenes/_scene.py, World; panels/model_kernel.py].
The density p(delta) is scaled so its centre sits level with k(d) on the kernel [panels/model_kernel.py, kernel()].
The paper writes the update as delta_e ~ q(. | mu, eta) with mu = lambda k(|d_e|) d_e [Overleaf sections/method_v2.tex:52]; “noise” on the slide is q.
The noise around the mean move is one of the paper’s noise families; the talk holds it fixed (Laplace in the paper’s selected models) [paper Methods].

text:
Some Learnings



Potential exposure \(\neq\) interaction
In experiments and online settings, relationship networks (proximity, following, etc.) define possible rather than actual interactions.


Model latent mechanisms
We can model what we don’t observe directly: we just need to tie it statistically to things that we do observe.


We direct our attention!
Even simple representations of attention can improve prediction and alter our conclusions.
